title: Four People, Four Answers
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The rumor reached the house before breakfast.

Someone had told a visitor that our household required every member to approve every romantic decision Jasper made. Another person had added that the arrangement meant all four of us were always together. By the time the story reached Mara's bakery, a stranger was confidently explaining the rules of a relationship they had never asked about.

Toph heard the entire account while waiting for bread.

She came home furious.

"Apparently," she said, slamming the door, "we're a committee."

Aang looked up from the kitchen table.

"What?"

"Somebody thinks our love life has minutes and a voting chair."

Katara set down her cup.

"Who said that?"

"Does it matter? Half the square is repeating it."

I felt my stomach tighten.

I had told each person I cared about that I was ethically non-monogamous and preferred polyamory. We had discussed informed consent, individual relationships, privacy, time, and the right to change our minds. We had never agreed that one partner could vote on another person's autonomy.

The rumor turned a careful collection of choices into a spectacle.

"What do you want to do?" I asked.

Toph folded her arms.

"Tell them where they can put their opinions."

"That's one option."

"It's a good option."

Katara looked at me.

"Before we decide what to say publicly, we should check what each of us is comfortable sharing."

Aang nodded.

Toph sighed.

"Fine. A meeting about not having meetings."

I almost laughed.

We didn't begin with a group statement. We began with individual conversations.

Aang found me in the garden first. He was sitting beneath the potato kite I'd hung by the window, looking uncharacteristically serious.

"I don't mind people knowing I love you," he said. "I do mind when they assume I can speak for Katara or Toph."

"I know."

"Sometimes I worry that being the Avatar makes people treat my answer as the household's answer."

"Then say it's yours."

He smiled faintly.

"That sounds simple."

"It isn't always."

He took my hand.

"I want to be open about us. But I don't want our private disagreements turned into stories people use to decide whether polyamory can work."

"Neither do I."

Toph found me next.

She didn't sit. She paced the room once, then stopped.

"I don't care if people think I'm difficult," she said.

"I know."

"I care when they pretend I agreed to things nobody asked me about."

"Then what do you want them to know?"

"That I choose my own relationships. That I like you. That I don't need permission from Aang to go on a date with you, and he doesn't need mine to ask for his time."

I nodded.

"And what stays private?"

She hesitated.

"The stuff that's ours."

I smiled.

"That's fair."

She leaned close enough to kiss my cheek, then looked embarrassed by her own tenderness.

"Don't make a big thing of that."

"Wouldn't dream of it."

Katara came to me after lunch.

She looked tired, not from the rumor alone but from days of coordinating water distribution after the bridge closure.

"I want us to be honest," she said. "But I don't want honesty to become a public inventory of who kisses whom."

"Neither do I."

"I also want to know if any of us is struggling. Not because we need a vote, but because we're responsible for how we treat one another."

I took her hand.

"You're allowed to ask for care without asking for control."

She smiled.

"Good. Because I'd like an evening with you soon, and I don't want to apologize for asking."

"Then let's plan one."

We did.

When we met together in the evening, there was no single speech that solved every concern.

Aang wanted openness without being made the household spokesman. Toph wanted to refuse the rumor loudly. Katara wanted a clear statement that did not disclose private details. I wanted the right to speak about my own identity without feeling as though every romantic decision belonged to the crowd.

We agreed on a short public notice.

Jasper and their partners are adults who make individual, informed relationship choices. No one in the household owns another person's consent. We do not discuss private relationship details with strangers.

Toph read it aloud.

"Needs more swearing."

Katara laughed.

Aang looked relieved.

I posted the notice the next morning with no names attached beyond mine. The others chose how they wanted to respond if someone asked them directly.

Most people ignored it.

A few looked embarrassed.

One person asked whether we could explain the arrangement as an example for their own relationship.

I said we could talk about honesty and consent generally, but not give them access to our private lives.

They accepted that.

That evening, the house was quiet.

Katara had made tea. Aang was repairing a kite frame. Toph was sitting near the open window, listening to rain on the path.

I sat at the table with them and felt the complicated warmth of belonging to people who had not become one person simply because we cared for one another.

Toph reached for my hand.

"Friday still ours?"

"If you want."

"I do."

Aang smiled.

"I've got tomorrow morning if you're free."

"I am."

Katara looked at me.

"And you and I can have the evening we planned next week."

"Yes."

There was no vote.

There was only each person asking, answering, and making space.

Later, when the lamps were low, I sat beside Katara and kissed her slowly. She laughed against my mouth when Aang called from the kitchen to ask where the spare tea cups lived.

"Second shelf," she called.

Toph groaned.

"He lives here. How does he not know?"

I laughed, and Katara kissed me again.

The private part of the evening belonged to the people who had chosen it. We closed the door without making the rest of our lives disappear.

The next morning, Toph found the public notice still on the board.

Someone had added a question below it: BUT WHO IS IN CHARGE?

She took the pencil and wrote:

EACH PERSON. TRY IT.

Then she came home for breakfast, extraordinarily pleased with herself.
